title: Practice Passage 4: The Secrets of the Indus Valley Civilization

passage.title: The Secrets of the Indus Valley Civilization
passage.sub_title: Exploring the sophisticated urban planning, engineering marvels, and mysterious script of one of the ancient world's greatest societies.
passage.content_html:
Paragraph A
Flourishing around 2500 BCE in what is now modern-day Pakistan and northwest India, the Indus Valley Civilization was one of the three earliest urban societies in the world, alongside Mesopotamia and Ancient Egypt. At its peak, this ancient culture spanned a vast geographical area, encompassing over a million square kilometres and supporting a population estimated at over five million people. Despite its size and influence, the Indus Valley remained completely forgotten by history until the early 1920s, when archaeologists began excavating the ruins of Harappa and Mohenjo-daro.

Paragraph B
What surprised early excavators most was the incredible sophistication of Indus Valley city planning. Unlike the chaotic, organic growth characteristic of cities in Mesopotamia, Harappa and Mohenjo-daro were laid out in a precise, grid-like pattern. Streets were wide and straight, intersecting at perfect right angles. Buildings were constructed using standardized, oven-baked bricks that were remarkably uniform in dimensions, a level of quality control unseen in other ancient civilizations. Most cities were divided into two main zones: a raised 'citadel' containing public buildings and baths, and a 'lower town' dedicated to residential housing and workshops.

Paragraph C
In addition to urban layout, the Indus people developed advanced hydraulic engineering that was far ahead of its time. Almost every house in Mohenjo-daro was equipped with a private bathing area and a toilet connected to a centralized sewage system. Wastewater from houses emptied into covered brick drains running along the streets, which were fitted with regular inspection manholes for cleaning. Water supply was secured by hundreds of brick-lined wells situated throughout the cities. The most famous hydraulic structure is the 'Great Bath' of Mohenjo-daro, a large, watertight public pool lined with bitumen, believed to have been used for religious purification ceremonies.

Paragraph D
Trade was a central pillar of the Indus economy. Archaeologists have discovered standardized stone weights and measures that indicate a highly regulated commercial market. The Indus merchants traded valuable goods, including lapis lazuli, carnelian, copper, and textiles, over immense distances. Seal stamps carved with animal figures and script have been found in ruins as far away as Mesopotamia, proving that maritime trade routes connected the Indus River and the Persian Gulf. This trade network allowed the civilization to accumulate wealth and support a prosperous urban middle class.

Paragraph E
However, one of the greatest mysteries of the Indus Valley Civilization remains its writing system. Thousands of seals, tablets, and pottery fragments have been excavated carrying a script composed of roughly 400 unique signs. Unlike Egyptian hieroglyphs or Mesopotamian cuneiform, this script has never been deciphered. Part of the difficulty lies in the brevity of the inscriptions, which rarely exceed five or six symbols, and the absence of any bilingual texts like the Rosetta Stone. Until the Indus script is decoded, many aspects of their political structure, laws, and religious beliefs will remain hidden.
